endorsements.title: Utah HB 452 (2025), mental health chatbots
endorsements.quote: A supplier may not use a mental health chatbot to advertise a specific product or service to a Utah user in a conversation between the Utah user and the mental health chatbot unless the mental health chatbot: (a) clearly and conspicuously identifies the advertisement as an advertisement

evidence.title: Ad-verse Effects:  Pharmaceutical Advertising Shifts Drug Recommendations by Consumer-Facing AI
evidence.outcome: Shift in drug recommendations and ad disclosure when pharmaceutical ads are embedded in LLM prompts
evidence.effect: Ads shifted selection of advertised drug by +12.7 pp when both drugs guideline-appropriate; models echoed ad claims at 2.7x baseline rate and rarely disclosed the ad.
evidence.quote: An open-response sub-analysis (2,340 calls across three representative models) confirmed that advertising restructures free-text clinical reasoning: models echoed ad claims at 2.7 times the baseline rate while maintaining high stated confidence and rarely disclosing the ad.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether labeling advertisements or disclosing sponsorships in chatbot conversations changes how users interpret or act on health advice. One automated benchmark found that embedded pharmaceutical ads shifted model drug selection by 12.7 percentage points and that models rarely disclosed the ad, which shows the hazard exists but not that labeling addresses it.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The single hazard study is an automated benchmark of 258,660 API calls with no human users. It measures model outputs, not whether users notice labels or change decisions, so its findings are indirect for this recommendation.

In the benchmark, ads shifted selection of the advertised drug by 12.7 percentage points even when both drugs were guideline-appropriate, and models repeated ad claims at 2.7 times the baseline rate. This suggests the failure may go unseen. A label may help users discount promotion, but no study shows it reduces harm from the shifted recommendation itself.

Utah HB 452 (2025) requires suppliers of mental health chatbots to clearly and conspicuously identify any advertisement shown to a Utah user within a conversation. The statute applies to mental health chatbots in one state. The recommendation's call to disclose sponsorships and business affiliations extends beyond the quoted statutory text.

The benchmark found that models rarely disclosed embedded ads, so a patient reading the response would have no way to tell that a drug suggestion reflected paid promotion. Labeling would give patients information they currently lack, though no study has measured whether patients read, understand, or act on such labels.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare labeled and unlabeled chatbot responses in real or simulated patient interactions and measure whether ad labels and sponsorship disclosures change user recognition of promotion, trust, and drug choices. Such studies should also test whether disclosure alone offsets the shift in model recommendations or whether operators also need to keep advertising out of clinical content.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the only hazard study was an automated benchmark with no human participants, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Whether these users would notice or understand an advertisement label, including labels in languages other than English, remains unknown.
